successor: Xiongnu (Late Xiongnu chanyu court under Huhanye)
notes: Chanyu institution continued: 60-54 BCE succession war among rival chanyus; Huhanye voluntarily entered Han tributary system (c.52 BCE), reunified Xiongnu after Han killed Zhizhi (36 BCE). 60 BCE is a period boundary. Second scholarly source not retrievable.

Same kingdom and capital continued: Ezana reigned c.303-c.350 across the boundary; kingdom flourished 1st-8th c. CE. 349 is a database period split. Home area 'Yemeni Coastal Plain' wrong (Aksum is in Tigray); 149 BCE start too early.

successor: Nara period (same Yamato imperial court, capital at Heijo-kyo)
source1: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara' (site 870) - https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/870/
notes: Same imperial government (Taiho code 701) moved its capital to Heijo-kyo (Nara), capital 710-784; pure period relabelling. Jinshin succession war 672 (Britannica 'Temmu') within 50 years. Balhae candidate irrelevant.

successor: Barakzai (Mohammadzai) Kabul principality under Dost Mohammad, later Emirate of Afghanistan
source1: Daniel Balland, 'Afghanistan x. Political History', Encyclopaedia Iranica I/5, 1983 (upd. 2018) - https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/afghanistan-x-political-history
notes: Kamran murdered vizier Fath Khan (1818); Barakzai revolt, civil war; Mahmud expelled to Herat 1819; realm split into rival principalities, Sikhs took Multan, Kashmir, Peshawar. Dost Mohammad held Kabul 1826. Sadozai Herat rump to 1842; British 1839-42 occupation targeted S.

successor: Kingdom of Germany (East Frankish kingdom) under Henry I, Ottonians
notes: Carolingian line ended 911 but kingdom continued: Conrad I elected, designated Henry of Saxony, elected 919 by Saxon and Frankish nobles. Conrad fought Saxon, Bavarian, Swabian dukes; Swabia and Bavaria withheld recognition until 919-921. End is dynastic change.

Ottoman province. Imam Yahya's Zaydi warfare forced recognition of his autonomy (1911); after Ottoman WWI defeat garrisons withdrew (1918) and Yahya ruled independently while Ottoman state survived to 1922. Region and Turkey candidate wrong; database end 1920 late.

source2: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Cyrus iii. Cyrus II the Great' - https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/cyrus-iii
notes: Persians defeated Babylonians at Opis, took Sippar and Babylon (Oct 539 BCE); Nabonidus captured and exiled; Cyrus became king of Babylon. Internal crisis: regicide/usurpations of 560 and 556 BCE and Nabonidus's long absence in Arabia.

successor: Seljuk Empire (Shabankara Kurds briefly held Fars c.1062)
notes: Tughril Beg entered Baghdad Dec 1055, imprisoned al-Malik al-Rahim: 'end of the Buyid amirate in Iraq'. Fars under Fulad Sutun fell c.1062 to Shabankara Kurds, then Seljuks. Decades of fratricidal wars and Turkish mutinies preceded.

source1: Cahokia Mounds Museum Society, 'Cahokia Mounds' National Historic Landmark brochure - https://npshistory.com/brochures/nhl/cahokia-mounds.pdf
source2: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Cahokia Mounds State Historic Site' (site 198) - https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/198/
notes: Archaeological phase without recorded central authority. Late Woodland villages at Cahokia (c. AD 700) were followed locally by Mississippian communities (800-1000); no documented population replacement. Continuity inferred, not explicitly stated.

successor: Holy Roman Empire under Frederick II (Hohenstaufen)
notes: Staufen side of 1198 double-election civil war. Philip murdered 1208; Staufen Frederick II elected 1211/12 (king 1212-50); Otto IV deposed 1215 after Bouvines. Faction's kingship continued past 1215. Brief 1208-11 lapse when partisans accepted Otto.
